## Live tool-call visibility and queued-job tracking

**This polling design is now the fallback/discovery mechanism, not the primary one —
see "Agent run streaming and the three chat surfaces" below, which describes the SSE
event stream that superseded it as the main live-progress channel.** Everything below
is still live and still correct (`GET .../agent/runs/current` still exists, still reads
`current_tool_name`/`current_tool_started_at`), it just isn't the whole story anymore:
`AgentRunCurrentOut` now also returns a `stream_url`, so the intended flow is poll
`runs/current` once to *discover* an in-progress run, then switch to its SSE stream for
live updates, rather than keep polling. `estimate.price_batch` (referenced below) no
longer exists — see "Parallel pricing execution" above — but `AgentRun.kind`/
`current_tool_name` and `Job.run_id`/`queued_jobs` remain accurate as a general
mechanism for whatever else queues a job from inside a tool-calling loop today.

The frontend previously had no way to show anything more specific than "thinking"
while a chat turn ran, and no visibility into `estimate.price_batch` work still
running after the main chat answer already returned. Three additive pieces close
that gap, all keyed off the existing `AgentRun`/`ToolCall`/`Job` audit trail rather
than a new tracking system:

- **`AgentRun.kind`** (`"chat"` default, `"price_item"` for a
  `price_one_estimate_item` pricing subagent — see "Parallel pricing execution")
  distinguishes a main chat turn from a pricing subagent's own run. Needed because
  both share `project_id`, and without this a concurrently-running pricing subagent
  could be picked up instead of the actual chat turn a poll is waiting on. This is a
  first-class column alongside, not a replacement for, the pre-existing convention of
  encoding a subagent's batch/item identity as text in `AgentRun.goal`
  (`"estimate.price_batch:{job_id}:item:{item_id}"`) — that stays exactly as it was.
- **Live "current tool" tracking** — `AgentRun.current_tool_name`/
  `current_tool_started_at` are set by `app/core/audit.py::set_current_tool` from
  inside `app/core/agent/tools.py::execute_tool`, the one function both
  `ClaudeProvider` and `OpenAIProvider` already call through for every
  client-dispatched MCP tool call. Set right before `mcp.call_tool`, cleared again
  (both fields back to `NULL`) right after, success or failure — a `finally` block, so
  a finished tool never shows as still in flight. Two small point-`UPDATE`s per tool
  call, chosen deliberately over a cheaper "set-only, clear when the whole turn ends"
  design: the latter would leave a stale tool name visible while the LLM is just
  generating text between calls, undermining the point of a live-progress signal.
  `GET /api/projects/{id}/agent/runs/current` (`app/api/agent.py`) reads this —
  returns the most recently started `kind="chat"` run still `in_progress` for a
  project, or `null` if none — for the frontend to poll (its own cadence, no
  backend-side polling interval imposed) while waiting on `POST .../messages`.
- **`AgentMessageOut.tool_calls`** (`app/api/agent.py::_agent_message_out`, shared by
  `GET`/`POST .../messages` so both get it identically) — every `ToolCall` row for
  that message's `run_id`, in order, as `{tool_name, display_name, status,
  latency_ms}`. Populated only for an assistant message with a `run_id` (mirrors the
  pre-existing legacy-artifact-inference conditional already in that function).
  **Web search is deliberately absent** — Anthropic/OpenAI execute it server-side and
  it never passes through `execute_tool`, so it's never logged as a `ToolCall` at all;
  confirmed as a decision, not an oversight (see Open follow-ups).
- **`display_name_for_tool`** (`app/core/agent/tools.py`) — a small pure function,
  `search_historical_material_price` → `"Search Historical Material Price"`,
  `create_rfq` → `"Create RFQ"` (a tiny acronym table, `{"rfq": "RFQ"}` today, extend
  as needed). Sent as an *additional* field alongside the raw `tool_name`, in both
  `tool_calls` entries and `runs/current`'s `current_tool_display_name` — the
  frontend keeps the stable machine-readable identifier and doesn't have to
  reimplement the formatting itself.
- **`Job.run_id`** (nullable FK to `agent_runs.id`) links a queued job back to the
  chat `AgentRun` that queued it, if any. Only `price_estimate_items`
  (`app/mcp/tools/estimates.py`) sets it today, via `current_run_id.get()` — the only
  job-creation call site that runs from inside an agent tool-calling loop; the other
  three (ingestion, `rfq.send`, quote regroup) are queued from REST routes directly,
  where `current_run_id` is already unset, so `run_id` stays correctly `NULL` there
  without touching those call sites.
- **`AgentMessageOut.queued_jobs`** — `{job_id, job_type}` for every `Job` with
  `run_id == message.run_id`. Paired with new **`GET /api/projects/{id}/jobs/{job_id}`**
  (`app/api/jobs.py`, generic — not `estimate.price_batch`-specific) returning
  `{status, attempts, max_attempts, result, error, ...}`. This is what lets the
  frontend show "still pricing in the background" after the main chat answer already
  came back: read `queued_jobs` off the message, poll the job's status while
  `pending`/`running`. `Job` has no `project_id` column, so the endpoint scopes via
  `job.payload["project_id"]`, matching every job handler's existing convention.
  **Deliberately not built here**: a reverse FK from `Job` to the `AgentRun`s *it
  spawns* (i.e. `estimate.price_batch`'s N `price_one_estimate_item` subagent runs)
  — without it, `GET /jobs/{id}` gives "batch running/done" but not "3 of 5 items
  priced" granularity. Noted as a follow-up, not a gap in this pass's own scope.

## Agent run streaming and the three chat surfaces

A real Server-Sent-Events architecture now exists on top of the polling design above,
and there are three distinct agent "surfaces" in this codebase, not one — none of this
is documented anywhere else in this file.

### The SSE run-event stream

`AgentRunEvent` (`app/models/audit.py`) is a new table: `run_id` (FK → `agent_runs.id`,
cascade-deleted), `user_id`, `sequence` (a DB `Identity()` `BigInteger`, globally
monotonic, unique, indexed together with `run_id`), `event_type`, a JSON `payload`, plus
the usual `created_at`. `sequence` is what resumption keys off. `TERMINAL_EVENT_TYPES =
{"final_message", "run_failed", "run_stopped"}` (`app/core/agent/events.py`). Other
observed event types: `run_started`, `tool_call_preparing`, `tool_call_started`,
`tool_call_finished`, `skill_selected`, `assistant_message_delta`,
`assistant_reasoning_summary_delta` (OpenAI-only), `provider_response_retry`, and
`project_handoff_suggested` (user-wide agent only).

**The start/complete split.** Every surface now separates fast DB prep from the actual
LLM turn: `start_*_run` persists the user message, creates an `in_progress` `AgentRun`
row, emits `run_started`, and returns immediately with `{run_id, stream_url}` — before
the LLM has produced anything. The caller backgrounds the real work
(`asyncio.create_task(complete_*_run(...))`) so the frontend can open the SSE stream
against `run_id` right away instead of blocking on the whole turn. All three surfaces
use this pattern: main chat (`orchestrator.start_message_run`/`complete_message_run`
— `handle_message` is now a thin synchronous wrapper over both, kept for non-streaming
callers), `user_wide_agent` (`app/core/user_wide_agent/orchestrator.py`, same two
function names), and `side_chat` (`start_side_chat_message`/`complete_side_chat_run`).

**The stream endpoints**, one per surface, near-identical bodies: `GET /api/projects/
{id}/agent/runs/{run_id}/events/stream`, `GET /api/user-wide-agent/conversations/{id}/
runs/{run_id}/events/stream`, `GET /api/projects/{id}/side-chat/runs/{run_id}/events/
stream`. Each resumes from a `Last-Event-ID` header or `after_sequence` query param
(header wins if further along), polls the DB every 0.5s, sends an `: heartbeat\n\n`
SSE comment every 15s of no new rows, and breaks the loop (emitting one final synthetic
`done: {run_id, status}` event) either on a `TERMINAL_EVENT_TYPES` row or when no new
rows arrive and `run.status != "in_progress"`. Real events are emitted as `id:
<sequence>` / `event: <event_type>` / `data: <json>` via `app/api/agent.py`'s
`_sse_event`/`_agent_run_event_out`, shared (not reimplemented) by the other two
routers.

**The old polling design coexists, as a fallback/discovery mechanism** — see "Live
tool-call visibility and queued-job tracking" above for what it still does and why it
hasn't been removed.

### `AgentRun.kind` values

`"chat"` (default — main project chat), `"project_setup"` (the `identify_scope` skill's
automatic orient/resolve turns, see "Thin mandatory project setup" below), `"side_chat"`,
`"user_wide_chat"`. `"price_item"` is a retired value that may still appear on old rows
from the deleted per-item pricing subagent (see "Parallel pricing execution" above) —
don't build new logic that expects to see it created going forward.

**The isolating rule is the same on every surface, and is the thing that keeps one
surface's run from being adoptable through another's route**: every stream/events/stop
endpoint re-derives the run by id and checks both project/conversation ownership *and*
`AgentRun.kind` before accepting a `run_id` — main chat's `_ensure_chat_run` accepts
`kind in ("chat", "project_setup")`, `side_chat`'s `_ensure_side_chat_run` requires
exactly `kind == "side_chat"`, `user_wide_agent`'s `_ensure_run` requires exactly
`kind == "user_wide_chat"`. A `run_id` from one surface 404s against another surface's
stream route by construction, not by convention.

### The three surfaces

- **Main project chat** (`app/core/agent/orchestrator.py`) — project-scoped, the full
  read/write tool catalog gated per-skill (see "Estimate categorization skill" and
  "Skill auto-detection" above); this is everything the rest of this file's "Product
  chat agent" section describes.
- **`side_chat`** (`app/core/agent/side_chat.py`, `app/api/side_chat.py`) — also
  project-scoped, but structurally read-only via a hard `SIDE_CHAT_ALLOWED_TOOLS`
  allow-list that excludes every write tool. Seeded with the main chat's recent history
  as read-only context (`_render_main_chat_context`, capped to the most recent 50
  messages) but never writes back into it — its own messages live in a separate
  `SideChatMessage`/`side_chat_sessions` table. Has no `GET` history-replay endpoint at
  all, which is why the terminal SSE event (`final_message`/`run_failed`) has to carry
  the complete finished-turn payload inline (session_id/body/tool_calls) — it is the
  only place a finished side-chat turn's content is ever recoverable from, not just a
  progress signal. **This entire start/stream/complete implementation is committed and
  live** (confirmed 2026-08-25 against `HEAD`: `app/core/agent/side_chat.py` defines
  `start_side_chat_message`/`complete_side_chat_run`, `app/api/side_chat.py` serves
  `POST .../messages/start` and `GET .../runs/{run_id}/events/stream`, and all three
  files including `tests/test_side_chat.py` are clean in the working tree) — the older
  synchronous, non-streaming `send_side_chat_message` it replaced is gone. Still not
  verified against a live LLM turn, per this file's own "How this was verified"
  convention.
- **`user_wide_agent`** (`app/core/user_wide_agent/`, `app/api/user_wide_agent.py`) —
  the one surface that is *not* project-scoped: cross-project, user-scoped, under `/api/
  user-wide-agent/conversations/{id}/...` rather than `/api/projects/{id}/...`. Its own
  tool set (`user_wide.py` in the MCP registry — `list_user_projects`,
  `get_project_overview`, `list_global_memories`/`write_global_memory`/
  `forget_global_memory`) is read-only over projects plus global-memory writes and web
  search; it cannot act inside a specific project. Instead it can emit a
  `project_handoff_suggested` event/block directing the user into a specific project's
  main chat to actually do the work — a routing surface, not a second place estimating
  logic lives. `list_memories`/`write_memory`/`forget_memory` (project-scoped, § MCP
  tool catalog / "Agent memory" below) and `list_global_memories`/`write_global_memory`/
  `forget_global_memory` (user-scoped, this surface) are two genuinely separate stores,
  not the same tool under two names.

## Agent memory

Freeform chat (never `categorize_estimate`/`determine_scope`/`price_estimate`) can save
a durable, repeating user/workspace preference or workflow pattern -- not a one-off
project fact -- so it's available in every future chat turn, on any project. Modeled
after ChatGPT/Claude's own memory feature, deliberately much smaller than an earlier,
abandoned `agent/memory-architecture` branch (6 typed memory kinds, versioned
revisions, hybrid pg_trgm+pgvector retrieval, a bundled Clerk multi-tenant auth system
this codebase doesn't have): **one plain table, three MCP tools, no embeddings.**

- **`AgentMemory`** (`app/models/memory.py`, `agent_memories` table): `scope`
  (`"global"` | `"project"`), `project_id` (nullable, null iff `scope="global"` --
  enforced by a DB `CHECK` constraint, same paired-condition pattern as
  `estimate_item_revisions`' unit-resolution constraint, backstopping
  `app/core/memory/service.py`'s own `_validate_scope_project`), `text` (capped 300
  chars, one plain sentence), `category` (free label, not enforced), `source_run_id`
  (nullable FK to `agent_runs.id`). No revisioning and no soft-delete status column --
  `forget_memory` hard-deletes; the `tool_calls` audit row is this feature's
  provenance record, not a stored status.
- **No retrieval machinery.** `active_memory_facts_for_prompt` fetches every
  `scope="global"` fact plus the current project's `scope="project"` facts, most-
  recently-updated first, capped at `settings.agent_memory_max_injected_facts`
  (default 40) -- fetch-all and inject, the same mechanical shape ChatGPT/Claude use at
  this scale (dozens of facts, not thousands). A separate
  `agent_memory_max_active_per_scope` cap (default 200, per scope bucket) rejects a new
  (non-update) write past it with a message telling the agent to `forget_memory`
  something first -- a runaway-write backstop, not a working limit any real workspace
  should approach. `agent_memory_enabled` is a plain kill switch (same posture as
  `agent_skill_auto_detection_enabled`) that disables only the per-turn injection
  fetch, not the tools themselves.
- **Three MCP tools** (`app/mcp/tools/memory.py`): `write_memory` (create, or update in
  place when `memory_id` is given -- the model's correct-instead-of-duplicate path),
  `list_memories` (read-only, for a dedupe check before writing), `forget_memory` (hard
  delete). **Freeform-chat-only by construction**: none of the three are in any
  skill's `SKILL_ALLOWED_TOOLS` (`app/core/agent/skills.py`), so they are structurally
  unreachable during a skill turn -- no exclude-list or runtime check needed, the same
  guarantee `categorize_estimate`'s hard allow-list already gives pricing-write tools
  (see "Estimate categorization skill" above). Regression-guarded by
  `tests/test_agent_tools.py::test_memory_tools_unreachable_during_skill_turns`
  (asserts disjointness against all three skills' allow-lists).
- **Prompt injection is two-tiered, deliberately different by skill.**
  `_build_system_prompt` (`app/core/agent/orchestrator.py`) appends the *facts
  themselves* (a plain bullet block) whenever `memory_facts` is non-empty, regardless
  of skill -- harmless read-only context, useful even mid-`categorize_estimate`. It
  only appends `MEMORY_TOOL_INSTRUCTIONS` (how/when to use the three tools) when
  `skill is None`, since that's the only turn kind where they're actually callable --
  telling the model about tools it can't reach during a skill turn would just be noise.
  `run_agent_turn` takes an optional `memory_facts: Sequence[str] = ()` param threaded
  straight into `_build_system_prompt`; `complete_message_run` (the chat-turn wrapper)
  fetches it via `active_memory_facts_for_prompt` and passes it down. The
  `scope_batch.get_or_create_scope_brief` nested `determine_scope` call (the only other
  `run_agent_turn` caller) doesn't pass it and simply runs memory-free -- accepted scope
  for this pass, not a gap requiring a fix.
- **Brace-safety is load-bearing, not incidental.** A saved fact is model-authored free
  text and could itself contain a literal `{...}` sequence. `_memory_facts_section`
  builds its block via plain string joining and is appended to `sections` *after*
  `SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE`/`CATEGORIZATION_SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE`'s own `.format()`
  call already ran -- never merged into that `.format()` call itself, which would crash
  every subsequent turn's prompt assembly on any fact containing `{`. Regression-tested
  (`tests/test_agent_memory_prompt.py::test_brace_containing_fact_does_not_crash_prompt_assembly`).
- **REST surface** (`app/api/memory.py`, `/api/memories`) for a future "manage
  memories" settings page: `GET` (optional `scope`/`project_id` filters), `PATCH`,
  `DELETE`. Top-level, not nested under a project, since global memories have no
  project to nest under. The chat agent itself only ever uses the MCP tools.
- **A real async-SQLAlchemy bug was found and fixed via live verification, not caught
  by any fake-session unit test.** `AgentMemory.updated_at` is a server-side
  `onupdate=func.now()` column (`TimestampMixin`); SQLAlchemy's default
  `eager_defaults=False` means an UPDATE (not INSERT) leaves that column *expired*
  rather than eagerly `RETURNING`-refreshed, and reading it afterward triggers a lazy
  reload that raises `MissingGreenlet` under the async engine -- reproduced against the
  real shared DB's schema on a throwaway Neon branch, both through `write_memory`'s
  `memory_id` update path and through the REST `PATCH`/`DELETE` routes (which
  originally serialized to `MemoryOut` *after* `session.commit()`, which
  `expire_on_commit=True` -- the default -- would have expired identically for every
  field, not just `updated_at`). Fixed two ways, matching the two failure sites:
  `write_memory`'s update branch and `patch_memory` (`app/core/memory/service.py`) now
  call `await session.refresh(row)` after `flush()`; both REST routes
  (`app/api/memory.py`) now build the `MemoryOut` result *before* `session.commit()`,
  matching `app/api/verifications.py::resolve_verification`'s existing (already-correct)
  ordering. No fake-session test can catch this class of bug -- a mock's `flush()`/
  `commit()`/`refresh()` are no-ops that never actually expire an attribute the way
  real SQLAlchemy does; only a live-Postgres pass exercises it. Worth remembering for
  any *other* in-place update elsewhere in this codebase that reads `updated_at`
  immediately afterward within the same session -- most existing code avoids this
  simply because its output types don't include `updated_at` at all (e.g.
  `VerificationRequestOut` only has `created_at`), not because the underlying pattern
  is actually safe.
- **Migration**: `alembic/versions/b1c2d3e4f5a6_add_agent_memories.py` (additive-only,
  one table). **Applied to a throwaway Neon branch of the shared DB this pass**
  (forked from and deleted after) -- confirmed the live schema (columns, both FKs, the
  composite index, the `CHECK` constraint) matches the model exactly, confirmed
  `write_memory`/`list_memories`/`forget_memory`/`patch_memory` against real rows
  (including the cap rejecting a write past `agent_memory_max_active_per_scope` and the
  `CHECK` constraint rejecting a validation-bypassed bad row), and confirmed all three
  MCP tools through the real `execute_tool`/`mcp.call_tool` dispatch path (not just
  direct Python calls to the service functions) -- **not yet applied to the actual
  shared/production DB**. Per this repo's live-DB verification discipline: apply
  `alembic upgrade head` to the shared DB as an explicit, separate step **before**
  deploying this branch's application code -- `complete_message_run`'s
  `active_memory_facts_for_prompt` call would otherwise `SELECT` against a nonexistent
  table on every single chat turn, degrading to the same generic
  `"Sorry, I hit an error..."` failure this function already produces for any other
  exception -- a full chat outage, not a memory-only degradation.
- **Not verified this pass**: a live LLM turn actually calling `write_memory`/
  `list_memories`/`forget_memory` off its own judgment through a real chat conversation
  (the prompt-assembly logic and the tool-dispatch/DB layers were each verified
  directly and separately, but not end-to-end through a real model deciding when to
  save something); the default `AGENT_LLM_PROVIDER=claude` path (this environment
  overrides to `openai`, same limitation nearly every other stage's live pass in this
  file has already noted). No consolidation/summarization job for when the active count
  approaches its cap -- a disclosed follow-up, not implemented this pass.

## Project ingestion readiness

Projects are created as lightweight JSON shells. Documents upload independently through
the direct multipart API, and chat is available immediately; there is no fixed
takeoff/spec/drawing bundle and no chat-wide readiness gate.

- **Readiness is derived, never stored.** `app/core/project/readiness.py` projects the
  current active document set into `missing | processing | ready | failed`. It reports
  counts for active, searchable, processing, and failed revisions. A failed optional
  source does not invalidate already published searchable evidence.
- **Setup waits for the active upload set.** Project setup orientation snapshots the
  project only after current active uploads finish processing. It defers while any are
  uploading/processing and reports a failure only when active sources produce no
  searchable evidence. Copy and status are about active uploads, not required roles.
- **Capabilities remain granular.** `/api/projects/{id}/ingestion` reports chat,
  document-search, visual-search, takeoff, and estimating capability separately, so
  clients do not infer one monolithic project-ready flag.

### Queue control-plane isolation and cancellation

Queue claims, 20-second lease heartbeats, and graceful lease releases use
`control_async_session`, a six-connection/zero-overflow pool separate from both normal
API/job-handler traffic and agent tool calls. Do not move those operations back to
`async_session`: the reserved pool is what keeps the 90-second leases renewable when
business traffic saturates its own pools. `/ready` validates both the main and control
pools plus every enabled coordinator's recent poll.

Heartbeat transactions are bounded to five seconds and track the lease deadline using
monotonic process time. Explicit renewal rejection or local expiry fences and cancels the
attempt without releasing/decrementing it; the coordinator waits at most two seconds for
cleanup before freeing its slot. A cancellation-resistant task is supervised outside the
slot and terminates the service after ten more seconds so Render replaces the process.
Deploy shutdown is intentionally different: it drains, then releases still-owned leases
without consuming an attempt. Preserve that lease-loss-versus-shutdown distinction.

## Thin mandatory project setup

Project setup starts only when the user explicitly chooses the `identify_scope` chat
skill after the current source snapshot is fully enriched. Document ingestion never
queues orientation on its own. Setup is a scope-decision ledger, not a project-fact
cache: specifications, products, conditions, and material requirements remain in
document retrieval.

- **Four MCP tools, all in `app/mcp/tools/project_setup.py`** (previously described here
  only as the abstract `project_setup.orient`/`project_setup.resolve` job/turn names —
  the tools themselves are named and allow-listed per skill):
  - `get_project_setup(project_id)` — read-only ledger dump (systems, status, questions).
  - `get_project_setup_input(project_id, setup_id)` — the orientation turn's input:
    source snapshot, deterministic type/CSI candidates, takeoff scope, prior decisions.
  - `save_project_setup_orientation(project_id, setup_id, scope_brief, systems,
    questions=None)` — the orient turn's terminal write. Caps at 12 questions, rejects
    vague defaults (`"unknown"`/`"unresolved"`), requires `scope_brief.evidence`. If no
    questions are pending, calls through to mark the setup `ready` directly; if
    questions exist, status becomes `awaiting_answers` and `project_setup.resolve` gets
    queued for later. This is the `project_setup_orient` skill's one terminal tool.
  - `finalize_project_setup(project_id, setup_id, systems)` — the resolve turn's
    terminal write. Requires status `awaiting_answers`, zero pending questions, and an
    identical system-tag roster to the provisional one; sets status `ready`. This is the
    `project_setup_resolve` skill's one terminal tool.
  Also relevant: `ask_user` (§ "Live MCP tool registry" above) is what the orient/resolve
  turns actually use to raise and durably wait on setup questions.
- **One normal orientation turn.** `project_setup_orient` reads `get_project_setup_input`'s
  compact bundle of deterministic type/CSI entities, grouped takeoff scope, the source
  snapshot, and prior decisions. It makes exactly one batched `retrieve_project_evidence`
  call, may expand a selected node, and may inspect at most one genuinely scope-changing
  visual page. Its eight-tool-turn limit (`SKILL_MAX_TOOL_TURNS["project_setup_orient"]`)
  prevents the old per-system deep-extraction behavior; its allow-list is
  `{get_project_setup_input, retrieve_project_evidence, get_document_context,
  inspect_document_page, save_project_setup_orientation}`.
- **Persisted output.** `ProjectBuildingSystem` rows are versioned by `setup_id` and store
  only the system identity, scope disposition/source, confidence, rationale, and current
  document-node evidence. `ProjectScopeBrief` is written by the same terminal orientation
  save and remains derived navigation context rather than citable Estimate evidence.
  There are no setup fact, specified-material, or extraction-unit tables.
- **Questions are part of setup.** Consequential contract/scope judgments use the existing
  `project_setup_question` verification kind, raised via `ask_user`. Every question gates
  readiness indefinitely until the user answers or explicitly chooses its resolving
  default; setup never applies a default because time elapsed. The final answer queues
  one `project_setup_resolve` turn, allow-listed to just `{get_project_setup,
  finalize_project_setup}` (three-turn budget) — it only reads the provisional ledger
  and finalizes resolved dispositions, nothing more.
- **Lifecycle.** The normal states are `pending -> orienting -> ready`, or
  `pending -> orienting -> awaiting_answers -> ready`; `stale` is terminal for that
  snapshot (only ever produced by a genuinely new snapshot hash, which always creates a
  fresh row instead of reviving the old one). **Correction — `failed` is not always
  terminal**: `get_or_create_setup` (`app/core/project_setup/service.py`) revives a
  `failed` (or `stale`) row back to `pending` when the *incoming* `source_snapshot_hash`
  matches the existing row's exactly — i.e. a same-snapshot retry after a failure reuses
  the row rather than treating `failed` as a dead end, which the older wording here
  didn't capture. Publishing a new source revision stales prior setup and supersedes its
  pending questions, but does not schedule the new snapshot; the user must explicitly run
  Identify Scope again. Old resolved answers remain non-authoritative orientation context.
- **Downstream boundary.** `get_project_setup` supplies scope decisions and user answers.
  When a current ready setup exists, categorization treats those decisions as
  authoritative. Missing, stale, incomplete, or failed setup never blocks
  `categorize_estimate`; it derives the system roster from searchable project evidence
  and the QTO instead. Categorization must still call `retrieve_project_evidence` for
  document facts. The same setup states never block `price_estimate` either; pricing is
  gated on deterministic completion of the current Estimate categorization, not on
  whether Identify Scope ran. `get_project_scope_brief` is read-only; there is no lazy
  `determine_scope` sub-turn.

## Stage 2-4: Estimate Item identification, structure, and labor basis

The next three stages of the 7-stage rehaul (identify the sellable Estimate Items a
sub delivers → structure their materials/labor/equipment/subcontract scope → determine
each labor activity's structural basis), all run inside one `categorize_estimate` skill
turn. This is the first stage that actually writes `estimates_v2`
content — and the first real v1→v2 tool replacement in the strangler-fig migration
agreed for this rehaul (see the earlier discussion in this file's history): `categorize_
estimate` now targets `estimates_v2` exclusively, not `app/core/estimates` (v1). The
deliverable is a fully organized, unpriced Estimate: real items, real components, real
labor bases, real CSI codes, real (optional) locations — with **no price, unit rate, or
productivity rate anywhere**, since no agent-facing type in this pass has a field for
one. Pricing (Stage 6) is a deliberately accepted gap until it lands on v2.

- **Identification is document-led, takeoff-validated, not takeoff-first.** An Estimate
  Item's identity comes from the design documents (a wall type, a door schedule entry, a
  ceiling system) — a takeoff row only confirms a system is present and how much of it
  there is; a bare takeoff row is never turned into an item on its own. The directive's
  order: read the ready setup/scope brief when available, otherwise derive the trade and
  system roster directly from searchable project evidence → *locate* (not read) the
  sections/sheets naming the building-system types this trade's documents actually cover → confirm
  against the takeoff → **research now, as the normal path**: one batched
  `research_project_documents` call reads the schedules/legends located in the step
  before and returns cited facts, skippable only by stating why in the narration before
  the first patch → adopt a location grain once → cut items by a fixed granularity test
  (different system type always separate; same type + different spec always separate;
  same type + spec separate only at the adopted location grain) → build components/labor
  basis → save incrementally → finalize once. A direct `read_project_document_section`/
  `inspect_drawing_sheet` call is an escalation from here on — a `stop_reason` showing a
  retrieval gap, a returned conflict, a flattened verbatim cell, or a gap a rejected
  patch exposes — not the way schedules get read by default. This was a live, fixed
  bug: an earlier ordering (locate-and-read together, before deciding whether research
  was warranted) let the agent read every schedule directly and then use the research
  step's own stated-skip permission to justify never calling it — confirmed on a real
  "categorize_estimate" run against project "Jack test 2" (~162s across 12 serial
  document tool calls, zero `drawing_sheet_observations` cached, since only the research
  pipeline writes that cache). See "Document research pipeline hardening" below.
- **Two coverage ledgers, not one.** Takeoff→items (every row allocated, excluded, or
  unresolved — this is the one `finalize_estimate_draft` hard-blocks on) and docs→items
  (every in-scope system type has an item, is out of scope, is by another trade, or is a
  real gap — this is the agent's own running account, submitted as `system_type_
  dispositions` at finalize, logged for audit only exactly like v1's `research_
  dispositions` always were — never stored as Estimate content, and not itself validated
  against anything, since there is no canonical system-type list to check it against).

### New v2 authoring/reading layer (`app/core/estimates/`)

`estimates/service.py` speaks only in raw UUIDs and a strict copy-on-write changeset
contract (`ReplaceSourceLinksChange`/`ReplaceSourceExclusionsChange` each replace the
**whole** version's list, never one entry) — nothing about that shape is safe for an LLM
to author directly, and until now nothing outside its own tests called into it at all
(confirmed via `grep` before this pass: zero external callers). Three new modules bridge
that gap, none of which existed before this pass:

- **`authoring.py`** — the only place agent-facing input (`ItemIn`/`ComponentIn`/
  `ComponentBasisIn`/`AllocationIn`/`ExclusionIn`/`RemoveItemIn`, all plain strings/
  numbers, no raw UUIDs) gets resolved into `VersionGraphDraft`'s UUID-keyed types.
  `build_changeset` is the main entry point: resolves a CSI code into its full
  MasterFormat ancestor chain (`09` → `09 22` → `09 22 16`, via `encounter_csi_node`, so
  sections roll up correctly — only the leaf gets the title, ancestors backfill on later
  reuse), resolves a unit string via `app.core.price_book.units.resolve_unit` (falling
  back to `raw_unit_text` when unrecognized, never rejecting), get-or-creates
  `ProjectLocationLevel`/`ProjectLocation` rows from an ordered location path (v2's own
  `create_location_level`/`create_location` are plain creates, not get-or-create —
  `authoring.py` adds the lookup-by-natural-key layer they lack), resolves an `R<n>` QTO
  alias against the project's takeoff rows in the same canonical `(created_at, id)`
  order used everywhere else in this codebase, and builds/merges the version's full
  `source_links`/`source_exclusions` lists (since those are version-wide, replace-only
  changes — a patch that touches one item's allocations must recompute the *entire*
  links list: keep every link untouched by this patch, drop the touched item/
  components' old links, append their new ones).
  - **There is no agent-chosen item/component key.** An item's identity is `uuid5` of
    `(project_id, slugify(name + location path))`; a component's is `uuid5` of
    `(item_uuid, slugify(name))`. The same name (at the same location) always resolves
    to the same identity on a later patch, including across a resumed conversation with
    no memory of prior tool calls — no separate key needs to be persisted or remembered
    anywhere. The deliberate tradeoff: renaming an item or component changes its
    identity too. This is not benign — confirmed live, a bare rename-via-upsert leaves
    the old identity's stale source links in place *and* double-claims its takeoff rows
    against the new one, since the old links never get cleaned up. The fix:
    `patch_estimate_draft`'s `remove_items` param (→ `RemoveItemChange`, which v2
    already cascades source-link removal for) — a rename is `remove_items=[old]` +
    `items=[corrected]` in the *same* call. The directive tells the agent this
    explicitly; there is no automatic detection of "this looks like a rename."
  - **Allocation conservation is hand-built here — v2 has none.** (v1 only has this
    check on its material-mapping path; v2's `SourceLinkDraft.attributed_quantity` is
    written verbatim, never summed or compared against `TakeoffLineItem.quantity`
    anywhere in `estimates/`.) `_check_allocation_conservation` sums every link's
    `attributed_quantity` per takeoff row across the **whole** draft (not just the
    current patch) and rejects a total exceeding the row's own quantity; a row claimed
    both by an unquantified ("full row") link and a quantified (partial) link in the
    same patch is rejected outright as ambiguous, before any DB query.
  - **Evidence validation** reimplements v1's exact whitelist (`{project_documents,
    project_document_chunks, drawing_sheet_observations}` + project-scoped existence
    check) natively, since v1's `_validate_evidence_refs` is private and raises v1's own
    exception type.
  - **Non-material waste normalization must be replicated here, not just left to v2's
    persist layer.** `service.py`'s `_apply_project_waste` forces every non-material
    component's `waste_application` to `"not_applied"` at persist time regardless of
    what was submitted (waste is material-only). Copy-on-write revision reuse
    (`_item_payload_equal`/`_component_payload_equal`) compares the **freshly submitted**
    draft against the **persisted, already-normalized** one — so without mirroring that
    exact normalization in `authoring.py`'s own `ComponentDraft` construction, re-saving
    a semantically-unchanged labor/equipment/subcontract/other component always forced a
    new revision. Confirmed live before the fix (every re-patch created a new item
    revision) and after (identical re-patch correctly reuses the existing revision) —
    this is the same caveat flagged during design review that "a caller that hand-builds
    an item draft ... will miss the item-level fast path even when semantically
    unchanged," now closed for the one caller that exists.
- **`readers.py`** — v2's only native read is `get_version_graph`; there is no
  `get_estimate`/`list_estimates`/`get_estimate_by_project` at all. `get_or_create_draft_
  estimate` is the lazy turn-start bootstrap (`get_or_create_draft_estimate` → `configure_
  project_for_v2` if needed → `create_estimate` with an empty graph on first use) —
  unlike v1's proposal workflow, nothing needs to run *before* the categorize_estimate
  turn starts; the tools bootstrap themselves on first write. `configure_project_for_v2`
  raises `ConflictError` for a project with any existing v1 `ProjectEstimate` row
  (**even archived** — its own docstring: "without migrating V1 estimate data"), which
  `get_or_create_draft_estimate` re-raises with a clearer message — a project categorized
  once under the old v1-writing skill cannot use the new one; there is no migration
  path, matching the agreed hard-cutover decision. `get_estimate_draft_state` resolves
  the graph's UUIDs back to human-readable form (CSI code/title, unit text, a
  reconstructed location path by walking `parent_id` pointers) and builds the
  takeoff-side coverage ledger by walking `source_links`/`source_exclusions` against
  each row's own quantity — **works even before any draft exists** (returns an empty
  state with the QTO catalog/`R<n>` aliases already populated, since that only needs the
  project's takeoff, not an Estimate) so the agent's very first read already shows it
  what `R1`, `R2`, ... refer to.
- The Estimate chat artifact is the canonical V2 workbook returned by
  `app.core.estimates.workbook.get_workbook`. `finalize_estimate_draft` returns an
  `AgentArtifactRef` to that workbook rather than constructing a second, legacy-shaped
  Estimate payload.

### Neon read-latency projection

Estimate versions are immutable, but the normalized V2 graph spans many revision and
manifest tables. Reconstructing that graph for every overview/artifact request used to
cost roughly 18 sequential SQL statements; the workbook then reconstructed it again
during approval validation. `estimate_version_read_models` is an additive, deterministic
JSONB projection keyed one-to-one by `estimate_versions.id`. The normalized tables remain
authoritative. Every version-creation path writes the projected normalized graph and its
approval validation in the same transaction; clone/restore copy the source projection.
`get_version_graph` reads the projection in one statement and only reconstructs from the
normalized tables for a pre-migration cache miss. That miss is persisted through a short
independent transaction because ordinary FastAPI read sessions do not commit.

After deploying migration `4d8f2a7c9e11`, run
`uv run python -m scripts.backfill_estimate_version_read_models` before routing user
traffic so pre-existing versions also receive the one-query path. The script is
idempotent and never changes authoritative estimate rows. A projection schema version
guards future shape changes.

The FastAPI lifespan also warms both SQLAlchemy pools before startup completes.
`pool_pre_ping` is intentionally disabled: against Neon it added one full round trip to
every checkout. `pool_recycle` replaces old sockets before checkout, and the frontend's
normal idempotent-query retry handles the rare optimistic-disconnect request. The `/`
skill catalog remains at its project-scoped URL for compatibility but is global metadata
and deliberately executes no SQL.

### New MCP tools (`app/mcp/tools/estimates.py`)

Three tools, deliberately different names from v1's so both stay registered without
collision (v1's tools remain available to external MCP clients and as a safety net —
only `categorize_estimate`'s allow-list stops pointing at them):

- `get_estimate_draft(project_id)` — the resume/orientation read: items, components,
  the takeoff-side coverage ledger (see above), validation issues.
- `patch_estimate_draft(project_id, items, exclusions, remove_items)` — the one write
  tool. Upserts named items (full component list each, matching v2's own aggregate
  semantics — `UpsertItemChange` carries an item's whole `components` list, there is no
  edit-one-component primitive), sets takeoff-row dispositions, and removes items by
  their old identity (the rename fix above). Surfaces v2's `ConflictError` (a stale
  `base_version_id` — read fresh, someone else patched concurrently) as a clear
  retry-with-refresh message rather than a raw exception.
- `finalize_estimate_draft(project_id, system_type_dispositions)` — terminal call.
  Blocks only on a takeoff row with **no** disposition at all (an `unresolved` row is
  allowed through and remains explicit in the draft's QTO coverage ledger). Returns an
  `AgentArtifactRef` to the canonical V2 workbook.

**Deliberately not built this pass**: a v2-native verification-queue kind for unresolved
rows. v1's `estimate_structure_issue` resolver is hard-coupled to v1's tables
(`app/core/verification/kinds.py`'s `_resolve_estimate_structure_issue` imports `app.
core.estimates.service` and writes `EstimateItem.user_confirmed`/`EstimateSourceExclusion`
directly) and cannot be reused for v2 subjects without a real rewrite. Unresolved rows
remain explicit in the draft's QTO coverage ledger, but a real
`estimate_v2_structure_issue` kind with its own resolver is still a disclosed follow-up,
not silently dropped.

### The retired "optimized" execution mode

`categorize_estimate` no longer runs the old v1-specific QTO-alias-substitution/preload
path (`app.core.agent.estimate_references` and friends) — the v2 tools take plain
`R<n>` strings directly and self-bootstrap the estimate lazily, so there's nothing to
preload. That machinery is left physically in place but unreachable, and ripping it out
is a disclosed, separate follow-up (see Open Follow-ups). Two of its user-facing
behaviors had to be restored directly in `complete_message_run`, just not through the
retired machinery: closing prose after `finalize_estimate_draft` succeeds, and
attaching the Estimate artifact (since `display_artifact` isn't in this skill's
allow-list). Full design writeup:
`docs/history/v1-tool-surface-and-retired-designs.md`.

### `categorize_estimate` latency pass — partial success, resolution caching, unit fixes

A real `categorize_estimate` run (project "Jack Test 3") took **17.9 minutes**
(`agent_runs.id=b3426729-...`). Output quality was excellent (13 document-derived
items, 39/39 takeoff rows allocated, 0 validation issues) — this was purely a
latency/cost problem, diagnosed from `agent_runs`/`tool_calls`/`llm_calls` directly:
**29% of the run (509s) was `patch_estimate_draft` retrying after rejection** — three
times, all traceable to `unrecognized result unit 'pieces'`/`'piece'`, then a
follow-on pydantic basis error once the model dropped `result_unit` entirely after two
failures. 50% of the run's output tokens went into payloads that were entirely thrown
away, since the tool was all-or-nothing. Separately, 16% (175s) was a nested
`determine_scope` turn computed synchronously on the critical path, and a further 7%
(80s) was `categorize_estimate` re-running the *same* document-orientation reads the
nested turn had just done. Fixed on four fronts, all in `app/core/estimates/`
(**not** `app/core/estimates_v2/` — see the note on that stale path below):

- **Unit resolution.** `resolve_unit` (`app/core/price_book/units.py`) tried only an
  exact code/alias match; no plural of any unit resolved (`sheet` worked, `sheets`
  didn't). Added a trailing-plural-strip fallback (`_singular_candidates`, tried only
  on a miss) plus a migration (`alembic/versions/965a28c7bc68_add_piece_unit_
  aliases.py`) seeding `PIECE`/`PIECES`/`PC`/`PCS` → `EA` — this project's takeoff
  used `pieces` as its unit on 20 of 39 rows, which had no mapping at all despite `EA`
  already existing. Applied to the shared DB (purely additive).
- **Validation errors now enumerate the valid set.** The model sees the full,
  untruncated `str()` of a raised `ValidationError` (confirmed by tracing
  `run_logged_tool`'s error path → FastMCP's `ToolError` → the provider — no
  truncation anywhere in that chain), so a message that only names the *bad* value
  and never the *valid* ones wastes a full round trip on a guess.
  `_resolve_controlled_unit_id`, `_resolve_qto_ref`, and the `remove_items` miss in
  `authoring.py` all now name what would have worked.
- **`patch_estimate_draft` supports per-item partial success.** A bad unit/basis/
  evidence citation on one item no longer discards the whole batch. `build_changeset`
  (`app/core/estimates/authoring.py`) resolves each item independently via
  `_resolve_item`/`_resolve_component` into a self-contained `_ItemBundle` — nothing
  touches the changeset's shared accumulators until a bundle is known to have
  succeeded, so a caught failure can never leave an item half-applied. Evidence
  existence-checking (`_evidence_existence_errors`) and allocation conservation
  (`check_allocation_conservation`, now a pure function taking a pre-fetched
  `rows_by_id`) both return per-id/per-row failures instead of raising, so
  `build_changeset` can attribute a failure back to the specific contributing item(s)
  — including an attribution *loop* for allocation conservation, since dropping one
  item restores links that can push a different row over. Returns
  `ChangesetBuild(changeset, base_graph, rejections: list[PatchRejection])`; raises
  only when *nothing* survived, with every rejection reason inlined in one message.
  Two no-op guards matter here and were both live-verified: if every item is rejected
  and nothing is removed, `full_links` would equal the unchanged base graph, and
  emitting a no-op `ReplaceSourceLinksChange` anyway would make `commit_changeset`
  raise `"changeset does not change the estimate"` — losing the whole rejection list
  in the resulting rollback; same for exclusions re-stating an identical existing
  disposition. `patch_estimate_draft` (`app/mcp/tools/estimates.py`) now returns
  `PatchEstimateDraftOut` (`EstimateDraftStateOut` plus `rejected_items`) instead of
  the bare read type, and logs rejections via `run_logged_tool`'s `result_payload`
  hook for audit. `EstimateDraftStateOut` itself is unchanged — a permanently-empty
  `rejected_items` field there would be schema noise on `get_estimate_draft`'s hot
  read path.
- **`ResolutionCache`** (`app/core/estimates/authoring.py`) memoizes CSI-node, unit,
  and location resolution for the lifetime of one `build_changeset` call —
  request-scoped by construction (never module-level/`ContextVar`/`lru_cache`, since
  these are per-project rows). Unit misses are cached too, not just hits, since a miss
  costs two queries and misses are exactly the strings an agent repeats across many
  components. `encounter_csi_node` (`app/core/estimates/service.py`) gained an
  optional `system_id` param (default `None` — every pre-existing call site
  unaffected) so the `ClassificationSystem` row, previously re-looked-up on *every*
  call, is fetched once per patch via the new `get_csi_system_id`.
  `commit_changeset` gained `base_graph: VersionGraphDraft | None = None`, skipping
  its own otherwise-duplicate `get_version_graph` fetch of the exact graph
  `build_changeset` already has; `apply_pricing_batch` (the other `commit_changeset`
  caller) got the same fix. Measured live: a 6-item patch with items sharing CSI
  code/unit/location dropped from 78 to 33 queries; a full patch→commit→read cycle
  confirmed correct end to end. The deeper win (`_persist_graph`'s own copy-on-write
  revision-creation loop, roughly another 25-30s/patch) was deliberately left
  untouched this pass — it has already broken copy-on-write reuse twice before (the
  Stage 2-4 waste-normalization bug and the Stage 5 pricing round-trip bug), so it's
  flagged for a separate, more careful pass rather than bundled in here.
- **`categorize_estimate`'s directive no longer re-orients.** Step 2 previously
  re-ran `get_project_document_summaries`/`search_document_understanding`/
  `list_document_understanding_cards`/`search_project_documents` from scratch to
  build its system-type roster, even though the nested `determine_scope` turn (step 1)
  had just read the same documents to write the scope brief. Verified live that the
  brief's own `evidence` already names the exact spec sections *and* schedule/legend
  sheets (a real brief's evidence cited `A7.10`/`A1.20`/`A8.12` sheets alongside CSI
  section numbers) with real `project_document_chunks` ids attached — directly usable
  without re-locating anything. Step 2 (`app/core/agent/skills.py`) now sources the
  roster from the brief first, and only issues a fresh locate call for a system type
  the brief's evidence doesn't already cover. `determine_scope`'s own step 5 was
  strengthened to require citing a schedule/legend's own section/sheet specifically
  (not just the governing division-level spec section) precisely so this handoff
  stays reliable. Confirmed against `tests/test_categorize_prompt.py`'s literal-phrase
  and step-ordering assertions and the 20,000-char prompt budget (assembled prompt:
  17,947 chars).
- **The scope brief is lazy.** The first active agent turn that needs one computes and
  caches it through `get_project_scope_brief`; there is no background warming job.
- **A pre-existing, unrelated staleness surfaced while writing this note**: this
  section (and "Stage 5" below) still reference `app/core/estimates_v2/` throughout —
  that package was renamed to `app/core/estimates/` in a prior commit
  (`ba25702`, "Delete the legacy v1 Estimate domain, collapse estimates_v2 into
  estimates"; internal `_v2`-suffixed identifiers and the `/estimate-v2` URL prefix
  were deliberately kept). Every path this pass touched or added uses the current,
  correct `app/core/estimates/` — the surrounding older prose was left as-is, since
  a full path-reference sweep across these two sections is a separate, larger cleanup
  from this pass's own scope.
- **New unit test coverage** (`tests/test_estimates_v2_authoring.py`,
  `tests/test_units.py`): `check_allocation_conservation`'s full branch set
  (over-allocation, the wholly/partially-claimed ambiguity, the tolerance boundary,
  a wrong-project row, multiple independently-violated rows) now runs with no DB

## Stage 5: interactive pricing

The fifth stage of the 7-stage rehaul: filling in `selected_pricing` on the unpriced
`estimates_v2` structure Stage 2-4 produces. The product rule, from the user: **the LLM
must never invent a price, wage, or productivity number.** It looks them up in a real
price book by reference; when the price book has no answer it asks the user in chat,
the user answers in a later message, and pricing resumes automatically — no background
batch, no separate "resume" affordance, just the next chat turn.

- **Enforcement is structural, not prompted.** `set_component_price`
  (`app/mcp/tools/pricing.py`) has **no parameter for a price, wage, hours-per-unit,
  or flat amount anywhere in its signature** — only reference ids
  (`material_price_id`, or `labor_productivity_id` + `labor_rate_id`), read by the
  backend off the referenced price-book row itself. `PricingSource="agent_estimate"` is
  structurally unreachable from this skill, the same guarantee `categorize_estimate`'s
  tool allow-list already established for structure (see "Estimate categorization
  skill"). The one number the agent may reason itself is a condition **multiplier**
  (`rate_multiplier`, `gt=0, le=3`) — because the price book cannot know site
  conditions — and even that is stored **separately**, applied on top of the referenced
  rate, never folded into it, and requires a basis + at least one document evidence
  citation whenever it isn't 1.0.
- **The multiplier declares which side of the labor calculation it hits.**
  `multiplier_applies_to: "hours" | "rate"` — `"hours"` for a productivity hit
  (restricted access, occupied-space phasing: the crew is slower) scales
  `calculated_labor_hours`, wage stays at book value; `"rate"` for a genuine wage
  premium (a night-shift differential) scales the extended cost, hours stay at book
  value. Neither `labor_hours_per_basis_unit` nor `labor_rate_per_hour` stored on the
  component is ever itself multiplied — both always reflect exactly what the price book
  said (`app/core/estimates/calculations.py::calculate_selected_pricing`). For
  `unit_rate` (material) pricing, a multiplier only ever scales `extended_cost`;
  `direct_unit_rate` stays exactly what was quoted.
- **The 4-branch material unit derivation** described in `MaterialPrice`'s own
  docstring (`app/models/price_book.py`) had never been implemented anywhere before
  this pass — `app/core/price_book/pricing_math.py::derive_material_price` is it:
  quoted directly in the estimating unit (unchanged) → quoted in the purchase unit
  (divide by `purchase_to_estimating_factor`) → quoted in a unit universally convertible
  to the estimating unit (divide by the conversion factor — price converts *inversely*
  to quantity, e.g. `$18/SY` with a SY→SF factor of 9 derives to `$2/SF`, not `$18 × 9`)
  → `unresolvable` (price `None`, surfaced for the agent to skip or ask about, never
  guessed past). A second hop repeats the same rule from the material's estimating unit
  into the pricing component's own unit, so callers never need to special-case "the
  component's unit already matches." `universal_factor` is a **non-raising** probe
  (mirrors `calculations.py::convert_quantity`'s compatibility checks, deliberately
  duplicated rather than shared — see the module's own docstring for why reusing
  `convert_quantity` directly would be wrong even setting aside the layering-cycle
  concern: "unpriceable" is a normal *result* here, not an exception).
- **Price-book search returns references, never numbers to retype.**
  `app/core/price_book/search.py`'s `search_materials`/`search_labor_activities`/
  `search_labor_classifications` (new this pass; the REST routes in
  `app/api/price_book.py` were refactored to share the same `material_match_clause`/
  `labor_match_clause` hybrid ILIKE+`pg_trgm` matching, per this repo's no-duplication
  rule) rank `is_preferred DESC, priced_at DESC` and **never** filter to preferred-only
  or sort by price — `MaterialPrice.is_preferred`'s own docstring is quoted verbatim in
  the module. Labor is two independent result sets (`activities` for productivity,
  `classifications` for wage) on purpose: labor pricing always needs two independently
  looked-up numbers, and an activity's `default_classification` is a suggestion only,
  never a binding.
  - **`csi_code`, on both material and labor activity search, is a ranking boost, not a
    hard filter** — fixed during this pass's own live verification (see "Verified live"
    below) after the very first live agent run passed a plausible-but-not-exact CSI
    code and got zero results for a material that had, in fact, just been priced
    correctly moments earlier by direct search. A material's own book classification
    routinely sits at a different CSI section than the Estimate component citing it
    (gypsum board priced under `09 29 00` while the owning item is coded `09 22 16`
    framing), and hard-filtering on the caller's CSI guess silently hid a real match.
    Both functions now order CSI-matching rows first via a `CASE` expression instead of
    excluding non-matching rows.
- **Direct price-book curation writes share one audited door.**
  `app/core/price_book/curation.py::record_user_answer` — the only function
  `record_user_supplied_price` (MCP tool) calls — resolves which Material/LaborActivity/
  LaborClassification the figure attaches to (get-or-create by name, same identity
  resolution the bulk-import path uses) then delegates to the existing
  `add_material_price`/`add_rate`/`add_productivity`, which already hardcode
  `source="manual"`. The user's own words are stored as the price/rate row's
  `notes`/`conditions` for audit. **Convergent resume, no correlation table**: since the
  explicitly curated answer becomes a real, `source="manual"` price-book row, the very next search for the
  same material/activity/classification naturally succeeds — no question↔component
  binding is needed for correctness, only for optional UX visibility (deliberately not
  built, see below). This path is only for a standalone request to curate the company
  price book. Estimate answers instead use immutable project-local inputs and require a
  separate explicit promotion before they become available to future projects.
- **`get_estimate_pricing_state` is the orientation-and-resume read**, always called
  first, every turn, including a resumed one — the model must never rely on what it
  priced or asked about from memory. Status is three-way: `priced` / `needs_price` /
  `blocked`, where `blocked` covers a component whose basis can never resolve into a
  quantity (an unresolved unit, an unknown quantity) — a categorization problem, not a
  pricing one, and without this bucket the agent would loop forever retrying a
  component no price-book lookup could ever fix. **Two resolution paths, deliberately
  not unified**: a labor component's driving quantity comes from the pre-existing
  private `service._basis_quantity` (read-only here); a non-labor component resolves
  its own `quantity`/`unit` directly (waste-adjusted for material) rather than reusing
  `_basis_quantity`, because that function only resolves a component's own quantity/
  unit when `selected_pricing.pricing_method == "unit_rate"` is *already set* — it was
  written for persist-time recomputation, not a pre-price probe, and calling it
  uniformly on an unpriced material wrongly reported every one of them as `blocked` (a
  real bug caught live before this split was added — see "Verified live" below).
- **`set_component_price` writes through the pre-existing, previously-uncalled
  `apply_pricing_batch`** (`app/core/estimates/service.py`, zero production callers
  before this pass) rather than adding a new `EstimateChange` type — it deep-copies the
  *persisted* graph and mutates only `selected_pricing` on named components, matching
  the copy-on-write discipline the rest of `estimates_v2` already follows. A
  `ConflictError` (stale `base_version_id`) is re-raised with a clear "read fresh state
  and retry" message; a `ValidationError` whose message says "does not change the
  estimate" (an identical re-price) is caught and reported as a benign no-op rather than
  propagated as an error.
- **The critical round-trip fix**: every new pricing field
  (`rate_multiplier`/`multiplier_applies_to`/`multiplier_basis`/`material_price_id`/
  `labor_rate_id`/`labor_productivity_id`) had to be added to *both*
  `SelectedPricingDraft`/`CalculatedPricing` (`types.py`) *and* `get_version_graph`'s
  reconstruction of a `SelectedPricingDraft` from a persisted
  `EstimateComponentRevisionPricing` row (`service.py`) — omitting it from the second
  place means a freshly-read draft never matches what's actually persisted, so
  copy-on-write's payload-equality check (`_component_payload_equal`) always sees a
  "change" and forces a new revision on every identical re-price. This is the exact
  same failure mode the Stage 2-4 waste-normalization bug was; caught the same way here
  (confirmed live, both the pre-fix failure and the post-fix correct no-op reuse).
- **Migration adds columns only** (`alembic/versions/b5c6d7e8f9a0_add_pricing_provenance_and_multiplier.py`):
  `rate_multiplier` (NOT NULL DEFAULT 1), `multiplier_applies_to`, `multiplier_basis`,
  and three nullable `ON DELETE RESTRICT` FKs into `material_prices`/`labor_rates`/
  `labor_productivity`, plus two new CHECK constraints on
  `estimate_component_revision_pricing`. Deliberately does **not** touch the existing
  `..._pricing_inputs` CHECK constraint — tightening it to require a reference id would
  wrongly reject legitimate reference-less `user_input`/`rfq_quote` rows written by
  other paths. Confirmed via `pg_constraint` before writing the migration that this
  table's *actual* live constraint names disagree with what `app/models/estimate.py`
  declares (a pre-existing, systemic mismatch across the v2 table set, documented in
  that model's own docstring) — never `op.drop_constraint` using the model's own
  constraint-name strings without checking `pg_constraint` first.
- **`validation.py` gained two advisory (non-blocking) checks**:
  `pricing_multiplier_undocumented` (multiplier ≠ 1 with no evidence) and
  `pricing_reference_missing` (`source="historical_match"` pricing with no price-book
  reference id at all). Both are advisory rather than blocking on purpose:
  `validate_graph` runs on every commit over the **whole** folded graph, not just the
  components a changeset touched, so a blocking check here would trip on any
  pre-existing historical_match row without a reference (v1-era or RFQ-sourced pricing
  has none) the next time *anything* on the estimate is committed. The real, structural
  guarantee is `set_component_price` having no numeric parameter — these are a hygiene
  signal layered on top, not a second enforcement mechanism.
- **`convert_quantity` gained a same-unit short-circuit**
  (`calculations.py`, before the `is_convertible` guard, after `is_active`) — without
  it, a component measured in a non-convertible unit (SHEET/ROLL/BAG/LS) could never be
  `unit_rate` priced at all, even with the rate already expressed in that exact unit.

### The `price_estimate` skill (v1 background batch → v2 interactive)

Rewritten in place, same precedent as `categorize_estimate`'s v1→v2 cutover — v1's
`price_estimate_items`/`estimate.price_batch` background-batch tool stays registered
for external MCP clients and v1 projects, untouched.

- **Hard allow-list**, not an exclude-list layered on the full catalog (same posture as
  `categorize_estimate`): the five `pricing_v2` tools
  (`PRICE_ESTIMATE_ALLOWED_TOOLS`, `app/core/agent/skills.py`) plus five read-only
  document tools needed only to ground a multiplier's required evidence citation
  (`get_project_scope_brief`/`search_project_documents`/`read_project_document_section`/
  `get_document_outline`/`inspect_drawing_sheet`). `SKILL_EXCLUDED_TOOLS` no longer has
  a `price_estimate` entry — the dict is empty now that neither `categorize_estimate`
  nor `determine_scope` used it either. Deliberately excluded from the allow-list, each
  for a stated reason in the code comment: every v1/v2 estimate-structure tool (this
  skill prices, it never restructures); `create_rfq`/`send_rfq` (RFQ-as-material-
  fallback is a disclosed later-stage follow-up); and — the one that actually narrows
  CLAUDE.md's general tier-1-historical-first flow —
  `search_historical_material_price`/`search_historical_labor_rate`, which return bare
  numbers with no stable reference id and would let the model retype one, defeating the
  whole reference-only mechanism.
- **No `SKILL_TERMINAL_TOOLS` entry.** An interactive turn that ends by *asking* the
  user a question has no terminal call to force an early stop on, unlike
  `categorize_estimate`'s `finalize_estimate_draft`.
  `SKILL_MAX_TOOL_TURNS["price_estimate"] = 30`, and `"price_estimate"` was added to
  `orchestrator.py::_run_agent_turn`'s `include_server_tools` exclusion tuple — a price
  comes from the price book or the user, never the web.
- **The directive's governing rule is stated first and hardest**: never invent, recall,
  or "reasonably assume" a number; every material price and labor wage/productivity
  must come from a price-book reference or an immutable project-local input. Nine
  numbered steps: read pricing state first every turn including resumed ones; on a
  resumed turn, recognize a bare reply to the assistant's own prior pricing question
  and call `apply_user_supplied_estimate_price`, then separately ask whether the user
  wants to promote it; skip
  `blocked` components and list them; material search (one lookup, choose by identity
  match then `is_preferred` then recency, never cheapest-because-cheapest, skip any
  `unresolvable` derivation); labor search (two independent lookups,
  `default_classification` is a suggestion only, `flat_hours` basis needs only a wage);
  the multiplier (basis + evidence required, roughly 0.85–1.35 absent an extraordinary
  cited condition, never a fudge factor); when the book has no answer, ask one clear
  question naming exactly what's needed and move on to the next component rather than
  stalling the turn, batching every open question into the closing reply; batch
  `set_component_price` calls; never claim a component priced unless the write actually
  succeeded.
- **Pricing readiness is deterministic and independent of Identify Scope.**
  `get_estimate_pricing_state` returns `categorization_readiness` from the current graph:
  an active draft must exist, it must contain at least one Estimate Item, every current
  QTO row must have an allocation/exclusion/unresolved disposition, and
  `validate_categorization_graph` must report no blocking issue. These are the same
  structural conditions enforced by `finalize_estimate_draft`; there is deliberately no
  mutable "categorized" flag that could remain true after a later breaking edit.
  `set_component_price` rechecks this result and rejects the write when it is not ready.
  The price skill still turns the returned deterministic blocker codes/messages into a
  natural-language explanation for the user before stopping.
- **`skill_router.py`'s `SKILL_TRIGGER_GUIDANCE["price_estimate"]` rewrite is the single
  highest-risk item in this pass, and was not deferred.** The old guidance told the
  classifier to leave any message naming a specific material/labor activity/trade
  unmatched (`skill=null`) — written for v1's all-or-nothing batch, where a subset
  request should bypass the skill and call the batch tool directly for just that
  subset. Left as-is, this old rule would have silently swallowed a **resume** reply
  too, since a real answer to "what's your rate for a drywall installer?" naturally
  repeats "drywall installer" — exactly the pattern the old rule told the classifier to
  leave unmatched. The rewrite splits into two explicit, independently-checked cases: a
  NEW request naming one specific material/activity/subset still stays unmatched (so
  ordinary chat can price just that subset directly with the same tools — an
  **unverified** assumption, see "Not verified this pass" below); a RESUME — a reply
  answering or declining a figure the assistant's own immediately preceding message
  asked for — must match regardless of whether it names the same specific thing the
  question did, and the guidance text says so explicitly with a worked example. Both
  `complete_message_run`'s `conversation` (fed to the turn itself) and `detect_skill`'s
  history slice include **both** user and assistant messages, with the assistant side
  being the real persisted final prose (not a placeholder) — confirmed by reading
  `_conversation_from_history_rows`/`_llm_content_for_history_row` before writing the
  guidance, not assumed; this is what makes the resume design possible at all, since the
  classifier and the turn both need to actually see the prior pricing question's text.

## Price-book search: word-level matching, match tiers, and a synonym dictionary

`app/core/price_book/search.py`'s `material_match_clause`/`labor_match_clause` used to
compare a whole query phrase against a whole material name -- an ILIKE substring hit OR
`similarity(name, query) > 0.2`. Both are whole-string comparisons, which fails in this
domain because price-book names are terse (`12-2 ROMEX`) while the pricing agent queries
with long descriptive phrases. Confirmed from the real "Azul Plan 1" session
(landon@hylang.com, project `31da0d5a-...`, read out of `tool_calls`):

| query | old result |
|---|---|
| `Revent RVS70 house trim 0.7 sone exhaust fan` | **0** (but `Revent RVS70 exhaust fan` -> 1, same material) |
| `12/2 NM-B cable` | wrong rows (never `12-2 ROMEX` — Romex *is* NM-B) [1] |
| `panel surge protective device` | **0** (book holds `Panel surge protection device`) |
| the 5-breaker `ETN 2P30A ... 2P50A ...` string | **0** |

[1] Correction, from a later head-to-head against the real book: `12/2 NM-B cable` is a
synonym PROBE this work added, not a query the session actually issued, and the old
clause returns ~10 rows for it rather than zero -- just never the ROMEX row, because
the two names share no letters. The failure is "cannot find the right entry", not
"returns nothing". The other three rows above are verbatim session queries with
verbatim zero results, and two of them are self-controlled: the same book answered
`Panel surge protection device` with 2 rows at 21:16:37 and `panel surge protective
device` with 0 at 21:16:58, and answered `Revent RVS70 exhaust fan` with 1 row ten
seconds after the longer phrasing returned 0.

The zero-result threshold made present materials look absent, so the user hand-typed
prices the book already had. **34 of 122 components were priced after two hours.**

### The four pieces

- **`search_terms.py` (new, pure logic, zero I/O).** Tokenizer, spec-token grammar,
  match ladder, scorer, tier assignment. The whole ranking algorithm is provable offline
  -- `tests/test_price_book_search_terms.py` replays every production failure above as a
  fixture. The metric that actually fixes the problem is **name coverage**: of the
  CANDIDATE's own tokens, what fraction did the (synonym-expanded) query hit. `12-2
  ROMEX` has two tokens; a ten-word query hitting both is a perfect match for that row
  regardless of how many query words went unused. This is deliberately NOT what
  `ts_rank_cd` computes (no corpus-IDF, query-side weighted), which is why ranking lives
  in Python over a small recall set rather than in the SQL ORDER BY.
- **Generated `search_tsv` columns** on `materials`/`labor_activities`
  (`Computed(..., persisted=True)`, mirroring `DocumentNode.search_tsv`). Postgres
  maintains them, so none of the seven Material write paths (including the sync,
  no-flush bulk-import cache) needs a sync point, and `ADD COLUMN` populated every
  existing row -- **no backfill script exists or is needed**. `english` for name/prose
  (bridges `receptacles`/`receptacle`, `protective`/`protection` for free), `simple` for
  identifier fields. `notes` excluded as noise.
- **`price_book_synonyms` + `synonyms.py` (new).** Flat rows sharing a `group_key`, the
  canonical term stored as its own row, so an N-way group is ONE indexed self-join.
  Expansion is **query-time only** -- a dictionary edit takes effect immediately for
  every existing row with no recomputation. Scope follows `unit_aliases` exactly (system
  rows `user_id IS NULL` + per-tenant rows, two partial unique indexes, deliberately not
  under RLS as controlled vocabulary); the reader filters BOTH sides of the self-join to
  `user_id IS NULL OR user_id = :uid`. Seeded with 53 groups / 182 terms.
- **The spec-token guard.** Tokens containing digits match EXACT-ONLY -- never fuzzily,
  never by plural strip -- and a same-shape/different-digits pair (`12-2`/`12-3`,
  `RVS70`/`RVS110`, `30A`/`50A`) forces tier `partial` no matter how well the rest
  scored. Grouped per skeleton, not per token: a five-breaker query that matches one
  real row is agreement, not four conflicts (that per-token version was a real bug,
  caught by test before it shipped -- it scored the correct candidate to zero).

### Tiers, and what the agent does with them

`exact` (full name coverage, no fuzzy match, no spec conflict) -> use directly.
`strong` (>= 0.6 coverage, no conflict) -> use, but disclose the unmatched query terms
when reporting. `partial` -> never price silently; show candidates and ask.

**The never-zero fallback is the AGENT surface only, deliberately.**
`search_materials`/`search_labor_activities` (what the MCP tools call) fall back to
un-thresholded similarity ordering when recall comes back empty, so an all-`partial`,
low-score set becomes the "the book probably doesn't have this" signal instead of the
old silent zero that made the agent hand the question back to the user. The REST list
routes (`GET /api/price-book/materials|labor`, the human curator's search box) do NOT
do this -- a person typing a genuine non-match should see "no results", not five
unrelated rows. Confirmed by the HTTP edge-case pass: the same nonsense query returns
closest-matches through the MCP tool and `total=0` through REST. Both surfaces share
one match clause and one ranker; only this fallback differs, and it differs on purpose.
Every candidate carries `match` (score, tier, matched/unmatched terms, `spec_conflicts`,
`synonyms_applied`); the rules live in the search tools' docstrings.

### `record_price_book_synonym` (new MCP tool)

Closes the learn-from-confirmation loop: when the user confirms a `partial` candidate is
their item under another name, the agent records it and every future search finds it
directly. Idempotent; refuses to re-point a term at a different group; writes a
user-scoped row only (a tenant's correction never changes shipped vocabulary); records
vocabulary, never a number, so Stage 5's reference-only pricing guarantee is untouched.
In `PRICE_ESTIMATE_ALLOWED_TOOLS` and step 2 of the price directive. Its docstring
forbids calling it on a `spec_conflicts` near-miss -- `12-3` and `12-2` are different
cables, not two names for one thing, and recording that would corrupt both.

### Latency: the fuzzy lane is escalated-to, not always-on

Measured on the real 2,637-material book (server-side `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, so network is
excluded): the full-text lane alone is **1.4ms**; adding one `<%` word-similarity probe
per recall term takes the same query to **29ms** -- the probes are ~95% of the cost,
computed per row. The old whole-phrase clause was **7.6ms**. So the trigram lane runs
only when the fast lane returned fewer than `_FUZZY_ESCALATION_THRESHOLD` (3) rows, and
is capped at the 8 longest terms. The common path is therefore ~5x FASTER than the
search it replaced, and typo tolerance is preserved for the queries that need it.
Note the planner scans by tenant and filters rather than using the GIN indexes at this
table size; the indexes are there for when a book grows large enough to change that.
